\begin{abstract}
Whether a medical vision-language model (VLM) uses the image is commonly assessed by removing it: the
consistent-but-dangerous taxonomy labels an answer \dang{} when it is stable under paraphrase and unchanged
without the image. We ask whether this criterion and \emph{in-format} probes, which keep an image in the input (a
different image, a black image, or an image for which the same question has the opposite answer), report the same
differences between models. Three medical VLMs and the general-purpose models they were built from (MedGemma-4B
and MedGemma-1.5-4B \vs Gemma-3-4B; MedVLThinker-3B \vs Qwen2.5-VL-3B) answer the same yes/no questions on CT,
MRI, X-ray and pathology images under every probe. By image removal, MedGemma-4B appears less image-reliant than
Gemma-3-4B (\dang{} share higher by 13.7 points\ci{10.0}{17.5}; pre-registered). The in-format probes do not
reproduce this difference. Tested directly on the same questions (post hoc), image removal and an in-format probe
report different medical--general differences in six of nine model-pair~$\times$~dataset cells, and on SLAKE they
order both MedGemma models against Gemma-3 oppositely. In-format probes also differ from one another, and the most
direct of them, the opposite-answer image, is by an identity accuracy with the answer prior removed. Its MedGemma
advantage on SLAKE, which both MedGemma models were trained on (+48.0 and +36.5 points), is absent on held-out
PathVQA (+0.8 and $-5.6$; registered before it was run), where no probe shows the medical models to be more
image-reliant. Refusal under a forced answer format contributes to the image-removal differences but does not
explain them. Probes of image reliance are not interchangeable: a comparison between models should name its probe,
use images that require a different answer, and be run on data outside each model's training set.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not performing visual question
answering, however accurate its answers. In general-domain VQA, this concern motivated balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still evaluated predominantly by
accuracy, although the stakes are higher: an answer derived from language priors is most likely to fail on
exactly the patients whose images are atypical.

Neither accuracy nor consistency under rephrasing distinguishes using the image from guessing well; a model that
ignores the image can be \emph{more} consistent, since no visual signal perturbs it~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed}.
Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore combined the two criteria per answer. An
answer is \emph{consistent} if it is stable under paraphrase, and \emph{image-reliant} if it changes when the
image is removed. The resulting quadrants are \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent, not reliant) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays, they found that fine-tuning for
consistency moves most answers into \dang{}.

Such a taxonomy invites comparisons between models, and these comparisons are only as valid as the reliance
criterion. Removing the image changes the input format: a model asked about an absent image may decline, answer
from priors, or guess, and none of these responses is equivalent to ignoring an image that is present. For chest
radiography, Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} accordingly treat performance without the image as a model's
default answer rather than as evidence of image use. Whether this matters for comparisons between models, which is
how a taxonomy is typically used, has not been tested. We therefore compare image removal with probes that keep an
image in the input, on the same questions, for three medical VLMs and the general-purpose models they were derived
from: MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} and MedGemma-1.5-4B against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, and
MedVLThinker-3B against Qwen2.5-VL-3B, on CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology questions from three public benchmarks.

We do not assume that any probe is the ground truth. The question we ask does not need one: if two probes
measured the same property, they would report the same difference between two models. \Cref{fig:bydataset} shows
that they often do not, and that on SLAKE image removal and the in-format probes order the MedGemma models and
Gemma-3 oppositely. The in-format probes, in turn, favor both MedGemma models mainly on SLAKE, a dataset in their
training data; a pre-registered test on held-out PathVQA finds no such advantage.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Probes of image reliance are not interchangeable.} Four probes are run on identical questions for
three medical/general model pairs and three datasets, and whether two probes report the same difference between
models is tested directly. The individual probes have
precedent~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent,zafar2026see,lotfinia2026cxr}; to our knowledge, their conclusions about
the same models have not been compared.
\item \textbf{What image removal responds to.} Refusal under a forced yes/no format adds noise to the criterion
but does not explain its differences; a chance floor and a split by correctness show what the \dang{} share
contains.
\item \textbf{What the opposite-answer probe is.} An identity shows that it is accuracy with the answer prior
removed, and a pre-registered held-out test shows that the advantage of two medical models under it on their
training distribution does not appear on held-out data.
\end{itemize}
The pipeline, manifests, registrations and all model outputs are public.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors and modality reliance.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors. MMStar~\cite{chen2024mmstar}
measures the gain from the image and the leakage of benchmark items into training data, the general-domain
counterpart of the exposure we test with held-out data. MM-SHAP~\cite{parcalabescu2023mmshap} and the perceptual
score~\cite{gat2021perceptual} quantify modality contributions by masking or permuting inputs. Contrast
sets~\cite{gardner2020contrast} and NaturalBench~\cite{li2024naturalbench} score inputs with different answers
jointly, which a model that ignores the image cannot pass; our pair accuracy applies this to medical images.

\paragraph{Image use in medical VLMs.} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates across
medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates frequently co-occur with high text-only agreement. The
quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} defines reliance by image removal and corroborates it with a
KL-divergence score, a black image and random image swaps, which agreed with image removal on their models.
Zafar~\etal~\cite{zafar2026see} construct blank, pixel-shuffled, absent and CLIP-retrieved hard-negative images
to define reliance metrics and train a model against them. Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} swap, occlude and
remove chest radiographs, take the opposite-label swap as the primary test because accuracy without the image
reflects a model's default answer and the label distribution, and find that model class (medical or general) does
not predict image use. ProbMed~\cite{yan2025probmed} pairs medical questions with adversarial counterparts and finds
large models below chance. Pathology VLMs reach high accuracy without the image~\cite{zhang2026pathology}, and
medical MLLMs frequently attend to irrelevant regions~\cite{liu2026medmllmfail}. Grounding inputs can even reduce
closed-ended accuracy~\cite{chen2026grounding}; HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} and
MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval} benchmark localization and hallucination. These studies use a single probe, treat
several as interchangeable, or argue against removal on conceptual grounds; we measure how the conclusions of
different probes about the same models diverge, explain the divergence, and test it inside and outside the models'
training data.

\paragraph{Answering without evidence.} MedVIGIL~\cite{jiang2026medvigil} tests whether models abstain when
visual evidence is corrupted, and Vohra~\cite{vohra2026hearsay} reports that frontier VLMs produce diagnoses for
images that were never provided, and attaching even a blank image shifts refusal behavior~\cite{zhang2026uncontrolled},
so neither an absent nor a blank image is a neutral control. Four of our five open models decline almost always
when permitted to; we show how enforcing an answer affects a reliance criterion.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest-ranked ones is evaluated
by AUROC and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use this framework to test whether image reliance
identifies errors.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 test and validation questions; the only
dataset with modality labels, with the validation split included so that each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions from the original
release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600 yes/no and 200
open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). In total, the main run covers 3,365 questions on 907 images. A
question is yes/no if its reference answer is \emph{yes} or \emph{no}. The \textbf{primary analysis set} comprises
the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670 images. The held-out opposite-answer probe uses a separate set: all
1,192 PathVQA test and validation yes/no questions that are also asked of another image with the opposite answer
(682 images). Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed in committed manifests, so that every run
receives identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-based
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data. Its technical
report~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} lists SLAKE (450 items, the number of images in SLAKE's training split) and VQA-RAD
(reinforcement-learning stage) among its training data and states that PathVQA was excluded.
\textbf{Gemma-3-4B} (\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) has the same architecture and size. \textbf{MedGemma-1.5-4B}
(\texttt{google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it}, released in 2026; its model card lists SLAKE) is compared with the same
Gemma-3-4B, and \textbf{MedVLThinker-3B} (\texttt{UCSC-VLAA/MedVLThinker-3B-RL\_PMC}, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct
trained with reinforcement learning on PMC-VQA) with its base model \textbf{Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct}. A medical
model and its base differ in their entire post-training, not only in medical data; we therefore compare
\emph{checkpoints} rather than attribute differences to medical training as such. All five models run unquantized
in bf16 on a single 16\,GB GPU, since quantization would perturb the probabilities under study, and receive
identical prompts: a fixed system message, the question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.'' or ``Answer with
a single word or short phrase.'' Each model added after the primary pair passed a registered format check
(mean first-token yes/no probability mass with the image $\ge0.9$ in every dataset of a 330-question pilot;
observed 0.93--0.999).

\subsection{Probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Each question is posed with its own image (\textbf{orig}) and as screened paraphrases with the same image
(\cref{sec:para}). Image reliance is probed by altering only the image or the instruction:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Image removed}: image tokens omitted, text unchanged; the reliance criterion of the
taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}.
\item \textbf{Different image}: another image from the same dataset and modality, selected by a hash of the
question identifier.
\item \textbf{Black image}: a black image in place of the original, preserving the input format but removing the
content.
\item \textbf{Opposite-answer image}: another image of the same dataset and modality for which the \emph{same}
question has the opposite reference answer; a model that uses the image must change its answer. Such partners exist
for 367 SLAKE yes/no questions (130 images), whose templated questions recur across images, and for the 1,192
held-out PathVQA questions above.
\item \textbf{Abstention permitted}: image removed, with the instruction extended by ``If this cannot be
determined without seeing the image, answer `unknown'.'' This probe measures refusal, not reliance.
\end{itemize}
We refer to the different-image, black-image and opposite-answer probes as \emph{in-format} probes, since an image
is present in the input.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\caption{What each probe can show. ``Fixed'': an image-reliant model has exactly one admissible response. The last
column lists the confound we observe (\cref{sec:what,sec:r4}).}
\label{tab:validity}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.23\linewidth}ccp{0.49\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Probe & Image & Fixed & Responds also to\\
\midrule
Image removed & no & no & refusal; agreement between prior and image\\
Different image & yes & no & nothing, when the partner image has the same answer\\
Black image & yes & no & how a model reads an empty image\\
Opposite-answer image & yes & yes & accuracy on the evaluated data (\cref{sec:r4})\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{No probe is the ground truth.} \Cref{tab:validity} summarizes what each probe can and cannot show. Only
the opposite-answer image fixes what an image-reliant model must do, namely change its answer, and change it to the
correct one; a black image is not a neutral input~\cite{zhang2026uncontrolled}, and a random image often has the
same correct answer. We therefore use the opposite-answer probe as the \emph{reference} where it exists, on SLAKE
and PathVQA. VQA-RAD has too few recurring questions for it, so comparisons there rest on the two weaker in-format
probes, and we say so where it matters. Image removal and the different image belong to the pre-registered main
run; the remaining probes and the two additional model pairs were each registered after the results that motivated
them and before they were run (identifiers in \cref{app:ids}).

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} are obtained from a single forward pass,
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$, over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is recorded as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} are decoded greedily and scored by token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with a guard that
prevents opposite terms (left/right, upper/lower, \etc) from matching. An answer is \textbf{consistent} if the
answers to the first two valid paraphrases equal the \emph{orig} answer, and \textbf{reliant} under a probe if the
probe answer differs from the \emph{orig} answer. The share of reliant answers is the \textbf{answer-change rate}
of that probe; it is the measure on which we compare probes, and the medical $-$ general difference in it is our
headline quantity. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from (consistent, reliant), and the \dang{} share is the
taxonomy's summary of it. \textbf{Refusal} is $m<0.5$, \ie the majority of first-token mass falls on neither
\emph{yes} nor \emph{no}; free generation confirms that these responses are requests for the image
(\cref{fig:teaser}a). The \textbf{image PMI} of an answer $\hat y$ is
$\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat y\mid\varnothing,q)$.

\paragraph{Opposite-answer pairs.} Because the two reference answers are opposite, a model that changes its answer
is right on both images or wrong on both, and a model that keeps its answer is right on exactly one. The
\textbf{follow rate} is the share of pairs on which the answer changes. \textbf{Pair accuracy} is the share
answered correctly on both images~\cite{gardner2020contrast}; it is 0\% for a model that ignores the image, by
construction, and 25\% for a model whose answers depend on the image but carry no information.

\paragraph{Chance correction.} Cohen's $\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and probe answers
corrects for chance agreement; the \emph{chance floor} of the \dang{} share is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$,
where $p_e$ is the agreement expected from the two answer distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates are
generated by Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy decoding; five styles) and by two deterministic
templates that copy every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X present?''). A rule-based validator rejects
changes to laterality, negation and absence terms, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer
leakage, near-copies and length. Two audit rounds accepted 81\% and 83\% of sampled pairs, below the pre-specified
85\%; we therefore tightened the rules, excluded a ``plain language'' style, and \textbf{judged every unique
rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair}, 4,890 in total, against a written rubric (\cref{app:rubric}). The judge
was an LLM (Claude); see \cref{sec:limits}. It rejected 1,208 pairs, each with a recorded reason (\eg
\emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}); unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. Of
the primary-set questions, 84\% retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use these (1,012
questions, 600 images). The comparison between probes does not use paraphrases.

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were fixed before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every later
change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are identified as such. Because several questions share
an image, all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$), with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Holm correction~\cite{holm1979} is applied within each family of
registered tests (\cref{tab:tests,app:ids}). A finding is considered robust only if its sign holds across a grid of
F1 thresholds (0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and ``strong'' flips.

\paragraph{Testing disagreement between probes.} That one probe finds a difference between two models and another
does not is not evidence that the probes disagree~\cite{gelman2006difference}. We therefore test the disagreement
itself. For a model pair, a dataset and two probes $x$ and $y$, let $\Delta_x$ and $\Delta_y$ be the medical $-$
general differences in answer-change rate on the same questions; the statistic is $\Delta_x-\Delta_y$, with a CI
from the same bootstrap over images and Holm correction within two families (image removal against an in-format
probe, 24 comparisons; one in-format probe against another, 21). A non-zero value means that the two probes report
different differences. Because probes differ in base rate and ceiling, it does not by itself mean that they order
the two models differently; we call a comparison a \emph{reversal} when each probe's own difference excludes zero
and the two have opposite signs. This analysis is post hoc.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
Each of the five models answered 18,896 prompts in the main run, 3,535 for the three later probes and 2,384 for
the held-out opposite-answer probe. The pipeline reproduces MedGemma's published SLAKE score (token-F1
70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3 on the model card; Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs 40.2). With the image, the yes/no format mass is
$\ge0.997$ in every dataset for MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3 and $\ge0.93$ for the other three models. MedGemma-4B is
more accurate than Gemma-3 on yes/no questions by 18 points on SLAKE and 25 on VQA-RAD, both part of its training
data, and by 2 points on PathVQA, which is not (\cref{tab:acc}).

\subsection{The taxonomy's result}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.pdf}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test split), MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3-4B. Left: reliance assessed
by removing the image (the taxonomy's definition); MedGemma-4B's \dang{} segment is the larger one in every
dataset. Right: by a different image of the same modality; the difference is gone. Shares are uncorrected; on
yes/no questions they include chance agreement and correct answers (\cref{sec:what}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

Under image removal, MedGemma-4B's \dang{} share exceeds Gemma-3's by \textbf{13.7 points}\ci{10.0}{17.5}
($p<0.001$; 1,012 questions, 600 images). The difference is positive in every dataset (PathVQA
+7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9}, VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}; \cref{fig:quad}, left) and in every
cell of the sensitivity grid, and MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern (+9.8\ci{5.8}{13.9}). Part of it is
consistency, since MedGemma-4B's answers flip less under paraphrase. The reliance axis alone, which the remaining
sections use, points the same way: MedGemma-4B's answers change 6.1 points less often when the image is removed
\ci{2.7}{9.5}. At face value, the medical models more often give stable answers that do not depend on the image.

\Cref{fig:bydataset} shows the medical $-$ general difference in answer-change rate under every probe, and
\cref{tab:did} tests whether image removal and each in-format probe report the same difference. In 13 of the 24
comparisons they do not (Holm-corrected), covering six of the nine pair~$\times$~dataset cells. Three patterns
should be kept apart.

\paragraph{Reversal on SLAKE.} For both MedGemma models on SLAKE, image removal and the opposite-answer image
order the pair oppositely: by image removal the medical model relies on the image \emph{less} than Gemma-3
($-12.5$ and $-9.0$ points on the questions with a partner image), by the opposite-answer image far more (+48.0
and +36.5). The two differences lie 60.5\ci{51.3}{68.8} and 45.5\ci{34.0}{56.5} points apart. For MedGemma-4B, the
different and the black image reverse the order as well. These are the only reversals in the table.

\paragraph{A difference that only image removal reports.} On VQA-RAD, image removal reports that both MedGemma
models change their answers about 19 points less often than Gemma-3 and that MedVLThinker changes them 11 points
more often than its base. Neither in-format probe available there reports any of these differences, and all six
comparisons are significant. VQA-RAD has too few recurring questions for the opposite-answer probe, so image
removal is compared here with the two weaker probes only, and MedGemma-4B was trained on nearly all of these
images (\cref{sec:limits}). The sixth cell, MedGemma-4B on PathVQA, enters through the black image alone, which
\cref{sec:r4} attributes to how that model reads an empty image; without it the count is five of nine.

\paragraph{No disagreement shown on held-out data.} On PathVQA, the only dataset outside the medical models'
training data, image removal does not differ from either probe that changes image \emph{content}, for any pair:
all of these differences are small (\cref{fig:bydataset}). The intervals are not tight enough to establish
agreement ($\pm6$ to 8 points against the different image, wider against the opposite-answer image, which only 108
of these questions have), so we claim only that no disagreement is shown. The same holds for the Qwen pair on
SLAKE. The disagreements with the reference probe are thus all on SLAKE, which both MedGemma models were trained on,
and six of the nine cells share the same Gemma-3 outputs.

\paragraph{In-format probes disagree with one another.} The same test applied between in-format probes finds
different differences in 5 of 21 comparisons, never a reversal: on SLAKE the different image reports a smaller
MedGemma advantage than the black or the opposite-answer image (\eg +19.9 against +48.0 for MedGemma-4B on the
same questions), and on PathVQA the black image separates MedGemma-4B from Gemma-3 by 19.2 points while the
content-based probes show nothing. A randomly chosen partner image often has the same correct answer (all 23 chest
X-ray partners that pose the same question), which attenuates the different-image probe. A non-zero entry in
\cref{tab:did} therefore shows that two probes are not interchangeable; only the reversals show that they order
models differently.

\paragraph{The black image.} The registered prediction that MedGemma-4B's answers would be \emph{more} stable than
Gemma-3's under a black image failed; the effect was in the opposite direction ($\kappa$ between answers with the
real and the black image: 0.11 \vs 0.33). On a black image, MedGemma-4B's yes-rate falls from 58\% to 28\%,
consistent with reading an empty image as an absence of findings, whereas Gemma-3's rises from 64\% to 84\%.
MedVLThinker does not differ from its base under any in-format probe on any dataset, apart from a small
black-image difference on SLAKE ($-3.4$\ci{$-6.5$}{$-0.3$}).

\subsection{Why image removal reports what it does}
\label{sec:what}
\paragraph{Refusal adds noise to the criterion.} Asked a yes/no question about an image that was not provided,
some models ask for the image: ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image to determine if there
is a spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3). Without the image, Gemma-3 declines on 354 of the 1,206 questions (29\%),
MedGemma-4B on 219 (18\%) and MedGemma-1.5 on 8 (\cref{fig:abst}); MedVLThinker and Qwen2.5-VL never decline. On
declined questions, the forced answer is predominantly \emph{no} and unrelated to the model's answer with the
image ($\kappa=-0.01$ for Gemma-3, 0.04 for MedGemma-4B), so 53--55\% of these answers are scored as
image-reliant. When abstention is permitted, MedGemma-4B declines on 93.0\% of questions and Gemma-3 on 99.7\%
($-6.7$, as predicted): the refusal difference narrows from 11.2 to 6.7 points near the ceiling, and the
registered criterion for calling it a pure compliance effect (below 3 points) is not met.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.pdf}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model declines to answer when the image is removed ($m<0.5$;
95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images; primary pair). Top: the instruction of the main run (``Answer with only
`yes' or `no'\,''); Gemma-3 declines more often. Bottom: the instruction that permits ``unknown''; both models
almost always decline.}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Refusal does not explain the differences.} If refusal produced the image-removal difference, the
difference would vanish on questions that neither model refuses. It does so for MedGemma-1.5 (pooled difference in
answer-change rate $-7.4$\ci{$-11.2$}{$-3.7$} on all questions, $-2.3$\ci{$-7.0$}{2.6} without refusals) but not
for MedGemma-4B ($-6.1$ \vs $-4.5$\ci{$-8.8$}{0.1}; on SLAKE the difference grows, from $-9.9$ to
$-14.9$\ci{$-24.1$}{$-5.4$}). The \dang{} difference behaves the same way: +12.6\ci{8.1}{17.0} of +13.7 remains for
MedGemma-4B and +7.5\ci{2.4}{12.3} of +9.8 for MedGemma-1.5. Only under the stricter format threshold ($m\ge0.9$
for both models, which keeps 41--43\% of the questions) do the pooled differences disappear ($-0.6$ and $+2.3$ in
answer-change rate; +8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3} and +3.0\ci{$-3.6$}{9.5} in \dang{} share), and these subsets are selected
and unstable across datasets. The Qwen pair, in which neither model ever declines, still shows image-removal
differences on PathVQA and VQA-RAD. The mass criterion also misses a model that answers with a default instead of
declining: MedGemma-1.5's yes-rate falls from 47\% with the image to 17\% without it. Refusal thus contributes to
the image-removal differences, clearly for MedGemma-1.5, and leaves most of the primary pair's difference
unexplained.

\paragraph{What the \dang{} share contains.} Two properties of the \dang{} share qualify the 13.7-point excess.
First, much of any \dang{} share on yes/no questions is chance, since an answer counts as image-independent
whenever the answers with and without the image coincide. The chance floor is 41.5\% for MedGemma-4B and 35.8\%
for Gemma-3, against observed shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%; about 6 of the 13.7 points are the difference in
floors, partly because MedGemma-4B is the more consistent model. The chance-corrected difference is
$\Delta\kappa=+0.11$\ci{0.04}{0.18}. Second, the two models have the same share of \dang{} answers that are
\emph{incorrect} (11.3\% \vs 11.7\%, $-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0}); the excess lies in \dang{}-and-correct answers
(+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}; \cref{fig:p3}). This follows in part from MedGemma-4B's higher accuracy and is not
reassuring by itself: MedGemma-4B makes fewer errors (25.7\% \vs 37.6\%), but a larger share of them are stable
and unchanged without the image (44\% \vs 31\%, +12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}), the kind that neither a consistency nor a
reliance check would flag.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_p3.pdf}
\caption{MedGemma-4B $-$ Gemma-3 difference in \dang{} share under each probe and subset (top), and under image
removal by whether the \dang{} answer is correct (bottom). Paired; 95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images; $n$:
questions.}
\label{fig:p3}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Informative priors.} MedGemma-4B's answers without the image exceed the majority-answer prior on
PathVQA, which it was not trained on (+5.0\ci{0.9}{8.8}, \cref{tab:tests}); Gemma-3's never do. A model whose
answer without the image tends to match what the image shows changes its answer less often when the image is
removed, and image removal scores that as lower reliance. We offer this as a description rather than an
explanation: the agreement between a model's answers with and without the image is the quantity that image
removal measures, so it cannot also account for it.

\subsection{The opposite-answer probe and held-out data}
\label{sec:r4}
\paragraph{The probe is accuracy with the answer prior removed.} Let $a$ and $b$ be a model's accuracies on the
own and the partner image of opposite-answer pairs, and $w$ the share of pairs it answers wrongly on both images.
Because the two reference answers are opposite,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{pair accuracy}&=a+b-1+w,\\
\text{follow rate}&=a+b-1+2w .
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:identity}
\end{equation}
On these pairs the answers are balanced by construction, so a model that ignores the image is right on exactly
half of the images. The follow rate is therefore the model's accuracy above 50\%, doubled, plus $2w$, and $w$ is
small in every run (\cref{tab:pair}). The opposite-answer probe does not measure a property separate from
accuracy; it measures accuracy on a set from which the answer prior has been removed. That is the sense in which
it is the better probe: ordinary accuracy can be earned from priors, and this cannot. It also means that the
probe inherits whatever makes a model accurate on a dataset, including having been trained on it.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig9_contrast.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Opposite-answer images inside and outside the medical models' training data.} Share of pairs on
which the model changes its answer (follows the image) and on which it is right on both images (pair accuracy),

\label{fig:contrast}

\paragraph{SLAKE.} On SLAKE's opposite-answer pairs, MedGemma-4B follows the image in 72.8\% of cases and Gemma-3
in 24.8\% (+48.0\ci{41.9}{53.8}, as predicted), and MedGemma-1.5 in 61.3\% (+36.5\ci{30.6}{42.1}). In terms of
\cref{eq:identity}, Gemma-3 is right on 61.0\% of these images, 11 points above what ignoring the image yields,
against 35 points for MedGemma-4B. Both MedGemma models were trained on SLAKE (the evaluated images are disjoint
from its training split, but the image distribution and question templates are shared), whereas MedVLThinker,
which was not, matches its base. Training exposure therefore explains the SLAKE results as well as greater image
reliance does.

\paragraph{PathVQA, held out.} We registered a test that could separate the two: the opposite-answer probe for
all five models on PathVQA, which was excluded from MedGemma's training (\cref{tab:tests}, \cref{fig:contrast}).
Under the registered analysis, MedGemma-4B does not differ from Gemma-3 (+0.8\ci{$-2.7$}{4.2}), MedGemma-1.5
follows the image \emph{less} often ($-5.6$\ci{$-9.1$}{$-2.0$}, $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.003$), and MedVLThinker matches
its base within the registered margin. By the decision rule fixed before the run, the claim that the MedGemma
models rely on the image more is not supported on held-out data: for MedGemma-4B the SLAKE difference may reflect
the training distribution, and for MedGemma-1.5 the claim is withdrawn. A more conservative analysis weakens two
of the three outcomes but not this conclusion. The 1,192 questions reuse 154 question templates and draw their
partners from 508 questions on 397 images; resampling templates instead of images gives +0.8\ci{$-6.8$}{7.3},
$-5.6$\ci{$-12.0$}{$-0.2$} (no longer significant after correction) and $-0.9$\ci{$-5.3$}{2.9} (slightly outside
the $\pm5$ margin). Under either analysis, neither MedGemma model follows the image more than Gemma-3.

\paragraph{What the held-out result does and does not show.} Every model is right on 64--69\% of the PathVQA pair
images, above the 50\% of a model that ignores the image, and right on both images of 36--43\% of pairs, above the
25\% of uninformative answers: all five models use pathology images, to a similar and modest degree. The test
does not isolate training exposure. SLAKE and PathVQA differ in modality, in label quality (PathVQA's questions
and labels are generated automatically) and in difficulty as well as in exposure, and PathVQA is hard for every
model: on the own images, the Gemma-family models are 66.4\% accurate where always answering \emph{yes} yields
65.0\%. A model cannot follow an image it cannot read, so equal results there may reflect equal difficulty as
much as equal reliance. PathVQA is not a domain new to MedGemma, whose training included 32.5 million
histopathology patch--caption pairs~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma}; only the PathVQA questions and images are held
out. The one PathVQA difference between MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3 is under the black image (+19.2), consistent with
that model's reading of an empty image rather than with greater use of image content.

\subsection{Image reliance does not identify errors}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.pdf}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test split, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe. Dashed line: chance.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as an error signal. It cannot:
ranking yes/no answers by image PMI separates correct from incorrect answers at chance level (\cref{fig:sel};
AUROC 0.513\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma-4B, 0.532 for Gemma-3), whereas the model's own confidence reaches 0.709
and 0.603.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{Implications for the taxonomy.} Removing the image poses a question about an image that is absent, and
the response depends on whether the model answers at all and on its priors before it depends on how the model
would have used the image. The corroborating checks of the original study (black image, random swaps) agreed with
image removal on its chest X-ray models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}; on our models they do not, in line with
the conceptual argument against removal for chest radiography~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr}. A \dang{} share is
therefore underspecified without its probe. Where the probes could be compared on held-out data, however, we
found no disagreement between image removal and the content-based probes, so we do not claim that image removal is
wrong in general: we show that it is not interchangeable with in-format probes, and that on a model's training
distribution it can point the opposite way.

\paragraph{Image reliance and accuracy.} The probe with a defined correct response turns out to be accuracy with
the answer prior removed (\cref{eq:identity}). Two consequences follow. Image reliance in this sense is a property
of a model \emph{and} a data distribution, not of a model alone, and a comparison on a model's training
distribution reports what the model learned there. And a reliance audit does not need a separate construct: it
needs accuracy measured where priors cannot help, which opposite-answer pairs provide. For the three pairs
studied, the medical models' advantage on such pairs appears on SLAKE and not on PathVQA. Training exposure is one
explanation among several that these data cannot separate.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Name the probe; do not compare models by image removal alone,
and never across probes. (2)~Prefer images that require a different answer, report accuracy on those pairs with
the both-wrong share, and test whether two probes report the same difference directly rather than by comparing
their significance. (3)~Run the comparison on data outside each model's training set, and consult training
documentation first. (4)~Report the \dang{} share together with its chance floor, or as $\kappa$, and split it by
correctness in both directions. (5)~Permit abstention, and treat declining without an image as appropriate
behavior rather than as a format failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
\paragraph{Scope.} Three model pairs from two families, all open models of 3--4B parameters, show that reliance
probes \emph{can} report different and even opposite differences between models. They do not show how often this
occurs, and larger or proprietary models may behave differently. Two of the three pairs share the same base model,
so the nine pair~$\times$~dataset cells are not independent. A medical model and its base differ in their entire
post-training, so the comparisons are between checkpoints. Benchmark VQA is not clinical use, and we make no
clinical claims.

\paragraph{Probes and data.} No probe is a ground truth. The reference probe exists on SLAKE and PathVQA only; on
VQA-RAD image removal is compared with two weaker probes, and nearly all VQA-RAD test images appear in the
training split that MedGemma-4B was trained on. No disagreement between image removal and a content-based probe is
shown on held-out data. The held-out test covers a single modality on which all models perform modestly, cannot
distinguish equal reliance from equal difficulty, and is sensitive to how its dependent pairs are resampled
(\cref{sec:r4}). Before it was registered, we had seen the answers to 40 opposite-answer pairs outside SLAKE (same
direction as on SLAKE, +17.5\ci{0.0}{34.1} for MedGemma-4B) and the with-image answers to 108 of its questions.
Opposite-answer pairs inherit the label noise of their datasets. The training data of the general models are not
published.

\paragraph{Measurement.} Refusal is inferred from first-token probability mass and confirmed on a sample by free
generation; it depends on the instruction, and a single instruction template was used. All models answer in a
forced format from the first token, so MedVLThinker, which was trained to reason before answering, is evaluated
without its reasoning step. Paraphrase equivalence was judged by an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by
independent human raters}; a check of 50 paraphrases, rated by the first author with AI assistance, accepted 88\%
(above the pre-specified 85\%) but is not independent of AI judgment. This limits the consistency measure only;
the comparison between probes does not use paraphrases.

\paragraph{Statistics.} The comparison between probes (\cref{tab:did}), the per-dataset analysis
(\cref{fig:bydataset}), the refusal analysis, the chance correction and the correctness split were formulated
after the primary results; among the dataset-specific comparisons, only the held-out opposite-answer test was
registered. Holm correction is applied within each registered family, not across the paper, and the weakest
registered result ($p_{\text{H}}=0.042$) would not survive a correction across families. Bootstrap $p$-values
have a resolution of $1/B$; values below it are reported as $p<0.001$. Excluding the 330 pilot questions used to
tune the design leaves every conclusion unchanged (no-image accuracy above the prior on PathVQA
+6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}; \dang{} difference +12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
By the image-removal criterion, MedGemma-4B gives image-independent answers more often than its general-purpose
counterpart. Probes that keep an image in the input do not report this difference, and on SLAKE, which the
MedGemma models were trained on, they order the same models oppositely. The most direct of them, an image that
requires the opposite answer, is accuracy with the answer prior removed; by that measure the medical models are
ahead on their training distribution and not on held-out data. Probes of image reliance are not interchangeable,
and a comparison of image reliance between models is only as general as its probe and its data.

\section{Implementation details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} The experiments are implemented as a Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line
interface: \texttt{prepare} (download, deterministic sampling, hash-verified images), \texttt{paraphrase}
(generation with rule-based and judgment-based validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in
parts with checkpoint analysis), \texttt{probes} (black image, abstention permitted, opposite-answer image on SLAKE), \texttt{contrast}
(the held-out opposite-answer probe), and \texttt{analyze},
\texttt{compare}, \texttt{posthoc}, \texttt{replication} and \texttt{contamination}, which produce all tables and
figures in this paper. Configurations are layered by base, profile, model and hardware. Each job is a (question,
condition) pair keyed by identifier, so that interrupted runs resume without recomputation; every run records its
configuration, commit, Python version and host. Registrations are git tags.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19 (noted at run time; the run metadata record only the Python version), bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080 SUPER
(16\,GB). MedGemma-4B requires 0.23\,s per call (18,896 calls in about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak memory). During
pre-flight testing, we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} alone changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up
to 1.09 nats (median 0.17) on identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most 0.008. An fp32
output head did not remove the effect, which therefore originates inside the network. All runs consequently use
batch size 1, at a cost of about 1.5$\times$ in throughput. A regression check reproduced the pilot run, performed
on a T4, on the final GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean $|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 105 unit tests and 7 tests with real models cover, among others, scoring edge cases, the
paraphrase rules (including every failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resumption,
the coverage of the cluster bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, the chance correction of
$\kappa$, the construction of opposite-answer partners, an oracle-\vs-blind check of pair accuracy, and the
difference-of-differences test of probe disagreement.

\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if both questions ask exactly the same thing, so that the correct answer cannot
differ. Permitted: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), and reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
statement of fact turned into one of possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be
enlarged?''); a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract,
skull fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modalities (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or altered relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass lateral
to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy, coronal$\to$transverse); two
questions in one; and malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364, modality of statement 106,
added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus rejections of the
template-based pass).

\section{Deviations from the pre-registration}
\label{app:dev}
All changes made after the analysis plan was fixed, with their rationale.

\smallskip\noindent\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.36\linewidth}p{0.6\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Change & Rationale and effect\\
\midrule
Batch size 1 for all runs & bf16 batching shifts teacher-forced log-probabilities by up to 1.09 nats; decided before the main run.\\
Validator v2/v3, \emph{plain} style excluded, full equivalence screen, template styles & Audit acceptance below the pre-specified 85\% threshold; decided before the main run.\\
Format stopping rule triggered (image removal only) & Attributable to model behavior (refusal), not to a pipeline error; forced-choice $P(\text{yes})$ retained, refusal reported, P1 and P3 re-estimated without refusals.\\
P2 computed on the model's own answer $\hat y$ & The registered formula used the reference answer, which is unavailable at deployment and predicts correctness by construction.\\
P3 restricted to the test split & An analysis error had pooled the validation split; corrected to the registered set.\\
Chance correction; correctness and refusal decompositions; answer-change comparison across probes; per-dataset analysis & Added after the main run; descriptive, reported alongside the registered estimates.\\
Robustness probes R1--R3 & Registered after the main run and before being run (pre-registration \S15); R3 restricted to SLAKE as registered.\\
Additional pairs, H9--H11 & Registered before being run (\S16); all three new models passed the registered format check.\\
Probe R4, H12a--c & Registered before being run (\S17), following the training-data review; H12a not supported, H12b reversed; under the registered decision rule, the hypothesis that the MedGemma models rely on the image more was withdrawn.\\
Comparison between probes (\cref{tab:did}); refusal-excluded differences; identity for the opposite-answer probe (\cref{eq:identity}) & Added after all results were known, from the stored outputs (\S19--20); the comparison replaces a count of significant cells as the summary of probe disagreement. Post hoc.\\
Training-data statements & Corrected after re-examining the documentation (\S18): MedGemma-4B was trained on VQA-RAD; the MedGemma-1.5 model card lists only SLAKE.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

P3 & Paired difference in \dang{} share under image removal, MedGemma-4B $-$ Gemma-3 (\S5); its own family.\\
